extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; readers of Hudson's introduction to Shakespeare and his contemporaries
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Hudson's introduction/study containing poetic cantos and prose criticism about poets (Shakespeare, Marlowe, Nash, Chapman) that articulates aesthetic qualities of great poetry and drama. Useful as a primary-text example and as informal critical guidance about what makes poetic/dramatic work powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendence / universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry or 'music' that 'laying strong hold on universal laws, ranges beyond these mud-walls of the flesh' — i.e., work that transcends ordinary human bounds and speaks to universal truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'What strange hints... there lie sealed in the magic pages of that music which, laying strong hold on universal laws, ranges beyond these mud-walls of the flesh, though dull wits fail to follow.' Also linked to finding 'an oracle in the books of Vergil, and an everlasting fount of science in the prophets.' (Use of classical/allusive scope to indicate universality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oracular or inspired voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A quality of being 'by spirits taught to write above a mortal pitch' — an inspired, prophetic, oracular tone that suggests the poet is moved by forces beyond ordinary craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrased as 'that spirit "by spirits taught to write above a mortal pitch"' and illustrated by 'oracular glories, visionary gleams' and moments when 'the mask moves, not of itself, and sings.' This favors language implying possession/possession-like inspiration when assessing poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounded truth / evocative depth emerging from chaos
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity of a work to produce 'some tragic semblance of a soul, some semblance of the rounded truth, a world glimpsed only through great mists of blood and tears, yet smitten, here and there, with dreadful light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued is a truth that is not tidy but emergent — glimpsed through chaos, mist, and sorrow; the passage emphasizes emotional complexity and moments of sudden illumination within tragic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity and elemental passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentic, elemental feeling: 'when a man, simple as all great elemental things, makes his whole heart a sacrificial fire ... There comes a laughter in which jests break up ...' — sincerity and elemental passion over mere cleverness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts 'simple' elemental devotion with 'clever' or vain affectations; authentic passion can transform tone and stakes (dreams to destructive action). Use this criterion to favor simplicity and wholehearted feeling over ironic cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid sensory and dramatic imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of concrete, sensory detail and dramatic tableau (as in the cantos: bees, honeycomb, moonlight, the Bo'sun stuck in honey) to animate scenes and evoke wonder or peril.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the poem: 'Black cakes of honey-comb', 'the Night-Wind ... Silvery tabors, purple drums', 'Up to his ears in honey!' — imagery and sensory concreteness are highlighted as central to creating vivid poetic drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful channeling or continuation of an author's voice
rubrics_metrics.description: When completing or responding to another's unfinished work, the successful continuation is described as feeling as if 'the hand that moved my pen was mine, and yet -- not mine' or 'the mask moves, not of itself, and sings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies a criterion for editors/continuators: fidelity to the original's spirit and voice (often described metaphorically as being 'moved' by that voice) is prized when finishing unfinished poems or plays.
